children: A blood plasma fractionation plant in Karawang, West Java, could make plasma-based medicines between 10.9% and 24.6% cheaper than imported equivalents,

The figures come from a study by the Indonesia Investment Authority (INA), the country's sovereign wealth fund, and the Institute for Economic and Social Research (LPEM) at the University of Indonesia's Faculty of Economics and Business. The study looked at INA's investment in PT SKPlasma Core Indonesia, which will process donated blood plasma into medicines that Indonesia currently buys from abroad.
Lower prices would deliver affordability benefits worth IDR1.43 trillion (about $77.8mn) between 2024 and 2037, the study found.

Oki Ramadhana, chairman of INA's board of directors, said the plant would turn blood plasma into essential medicines at affordable prices with a secure supply. He said it would also help build the skills of the local workforce.

Speaking at the launch of INA's second socio-economic impact report in South Jakarta, Ramadhana said the facility was the first and largest plasma fractionation plant outside China, and that INA had built it with its partners.
The study estimates that the investment will add IDR26 trillion in value to gross domestic product. It puts the direct and indirect fiscal impact at IDR2.44 trillion.
The project is expected to support around 7,221 direct and indirect jobs each year.
In a separate investment in the sector, as
reports, that Takeda plans to spend IDR539bn on a plasma bank in Indonesia, with technology transfer included.

title: Indonesia's plasma plant could cut drug prices 24.6%
